articles.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.snippet: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
articles.full_text:
AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
- Published
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.
Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
- Published1 hour ago
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
- Published7 hours ago
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
Strong jobs figures could ease market fears
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
articles.snippet: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.
articles.full_text:
Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
- Published
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways.
The 2026 winners who now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.
California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.
Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
- Published1 day ago
JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.
"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."
Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.
Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.
Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
articles.snippet: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
articles.full_text:
Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
- Published
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.
French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.
In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.
The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".
The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".
Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-RhÃ´ne-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."
Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene.
Earlier, French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
- Published
European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.
It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÃ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".
Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
- Published4 hours ago
A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÃ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.
Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaÃ (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".
In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister MicheÃ¡l Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÃ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÃ had evacuated its building.
The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
articles.snippet: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
articles.full_text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
- Published
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.
"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.
Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.
Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

articles.title: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
articles.snippet: The Trump administration had hoped the construction of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.
articles.full_text:
Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
- Published
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.
Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.
The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.
"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.
The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."
"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.
A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.
It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".
The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.
The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.
Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".
He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".
Opponents have strongly disagreed.
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego â they've been rejected."
Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.
Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office
- Published8 hours ago
Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.
Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.
It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (Â£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.title: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
articles.snippet: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.
articles.full_text:
Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
- Published
The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.
The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.
Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.
It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.
Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".
One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France â another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.
One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.
As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.
"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.

articles.title: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.snippet: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
articles.full_text:
Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
- Published
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” the attorney general said.

Millions fleeing Sudan’s war risk losing shelter as funds run low, UN warns
Fewer than 1 million of the 15.4 million people in need emergency shelter in Sudan have received assistance.
Millions of people in Sudan who have been displaced by the country’s civil war risk being left without emergency shelter due to funding shortages and depleting aid stocks, according to the United Nations refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration.
An estimated 15.4 million people across Sudan urgently need emergency shelter and basic household items, but funding shortages mean humanitarian agencies can prioritise assistance for only approximately 10 percent of those in need, the two UN agencies said in a joint statement on Friday.

So far, only 936,000 people have received assistance, leaving a large gap between needs and available resources, according to the statement.
Since war broke out in 2023 between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), about 8.6 million people have been displaced within the country, making Sudan the world’s largest displacement crisis.
Meanwhile, more than 4.6 million people have fled across the country’s borders.
More than 5.2 million people have also returned to their areas of origin, often finding homes, infrastructure and basic services destroyed, the UN says.
“For families repeatedly displaced by conflict, a safe place to sleep and basic household supplies are far more than everyday necessities,” the joint statement said.

articles.title: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.snippet: Russia is already using its new Rassvet satellite network — billed as a homegrown version of Starlink — for military communications over Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence.
articles.full_text:
Russia is already using its new Rassvet satellite network — billed as a homegrown version of Starlink — for military communications over Ukraine, aiming to make its strike drones more accurate and harder to jam, Ukrainian military intelligence told Reuters.
Russia has launched 32 Rassvet satellites into orbit so far this year in two batches in March and July, according to the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense (GUR). The Russian government said last month that Russia had launched more than 30 satellites.
That is a tiny fraction of the more than 10,000 satellites in the Starlink network, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, the military version of which — Starshield — operates in Ukraine but not in Russia. Access to SpaceX systems, which Moscow does not have, has greatly helped Kyiv in the war against invading Russian forces.
Moscow plans more Rassvet launches by the end of 2026 to expand the network’s geographic coverage, gradually bringing it closer to a full low-orbit satellite communications system, GUR said in a written statement.
“Russia is using the ‘Rassvet’ satellite system over the territory of Ukraine for military purposes,” GUR spokesman Andrii Yusov said in the statement.
“The constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory: communication is available intermittently when the satellites pass over the relevant areas.”
Russia’s defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia’s Scientific and Expert Council warned of the risks posed by Starlink on Friday and urged a quicker deployment of the Rassvet system.
RENEWED UNCERTAINTY OVER US SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE
Starshield has given Kyiv a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications.
Russian forces had been using grey-market Starlink terminals in Ukraine until Kyiv successfully lobbied SpaceX to disable them earlier this year, one of several factors that shifted battlefield momentum in Ukraine’s favor this year.
However, last month Ukrainian battlefield commanders unexpectedly saw speed limitations imposed on Starshield, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forcing the cancellation of some strike operations.
No explanation has been given for the temporary restrictions on Starshield, which came amid tensions with President Donald Trump’s administration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and have now been lifted.
While Russia’s territorial gains on the front line have ground to a virtual halt this year, it has doubled down on strikes against Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure and cities, using a new generation of jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly raised concerns about Russia’s attempts to build its own version of SpaceX’s network. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week imposed sanctions on 10 companies involved in developing Rassvet, including Bureau 1440 — the coordinator of the state-backed project.
Bureau 1440 has said it plans to create a constellation of more than 900 satellites by 2035. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters’ questions about Rassvet.
BOOST TO SURVEILLANCE AND STRIKE DRONES
The GUR statement said that Rassvet may provide Russia with two-way data exchange with its unmanned aircraft over Ukraine, allowing surveillance drones to transmit data in real time and pilots to adjust the route of attack drones during flight, reducing dependence on a pre-programmed flight path.
That could allow drones to adjust to changes in target location, or evade air defenses.
“In the longer term, this could increase the effectiveness of strike and reconnaissance UAVs and make it more difficult for electronic warfare and electronic intelligence systems to intercept them,” Yusov said.
Mykola Zientsev, a Kyiv-based security expert, said there were some signs that Rassvet was already having an impact on precision strikes by Russian jet-powered drones.
“In practical terms, Russia already possesses at least two high-quality satellite communications windows every day, each lasting more than an hour,” he wrote in a recent report. “That is enough to have operational consequences.”
GUR has published a list of 49 companies from Russia and Belarus that it says are involved in the project.
Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of GUR, said in an interview with Ukrainian media in August that Russia was launching the Rassvet system much faster than originally planned and Ukraine was already discussing ways to counter it.
Ukraine said in August it had carried out a long-range missile attack against the Progress rocket and space center in Russia’s Samara region, which produces rockets used to launch Rassvet satellites.
Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Washington, has urged the U.S. to impose its own sanctions on Rassvet companies. He also told Reuters that Russia was developing the Starlink analogue using Chinese components.
The U.S. Treasury Department had no comment on Ukraine’s push for further sanctions.

articles.title: US European Command launches vigilance campaign as hybrid threats mount
articles.snippet: U.S. European Command is calling on U.S. troops, family members, and civilian employees to stay alert for suspicious behavior and to cover their digital tracks while moving around Europe.
articles.full_text:
U.S. European Command is calling on troops, family members, and civilian employees to watch for suspicious behavior on and off military installations and to cover their digital tracks while moving around Europe.
Branded “See Something, Do Something,” the initiative is meant “to foster a proactive mindset” toward security and force protection, the command said this week. The announcement comes amid heightened concern about drone incursions and other hybrid threats to U.S. and allied military forces around Europe.
The initiative emphasizes protecting U.S. personnel and their families “as a shared responsibility vital to sustaining long-term combat readiness alongside global partners.” It encourages members of U.S. military communities to stay alert while in crowded public areas, like transit hubs, and report any “unusual behavior or unattended items” to military police or local authorities.
Troops and their families are also “urged” to practice “rigorous digital discipline” by reviewing their social-media privacy settings, disabling geotagging on fitness apps and mobile devices, and avoiding posting information about their locations and travels online. The announcement also cites a recommendation from security experts to vary daily commuting routes, travel times, and off-base activities “to reduce predictability.”
U.S. personnel and their families “are our most precious asset, and their safety is our highest priority,” Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, commander of U.S. European Command, said in the announcement. “By embracing a proactive security mindset and enhancing collective vigilance, we build a stronger force protection environment that keeps us safe and ready.”
European Command did not identify a specific threat that prompted the campaign, but it comes amid increased concern about “hybrid warfare,” — malign activity below the threshold of war that often lacks a clear perpetrator — involving Russia and targeting U.S. forces and NATO allies.
Russian misinformation and intimidation directed against U.S. military personnel and their families using social media and hacking has been a longstanding concern. But since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, that hybrid activity has become more aggressive and disruptive. A number of undersea pipelines and cables have been affected by what Western officials believe to be sabotage; GPS jamming and spoofing are more frequent, and drone incursions around sensitive sites, like military bases and airports, have increased.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating a failed attack with explosive-laden drones at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, which is a key logistical hub for Western supplies to Ukraine. Later in September, a tip about suspicious vehicles near the airbase RAF Fairford led to the arrest of several men in relation to a suspected terrorist plot in which British officials say Iran may have been involved. The incident prompted the US to remove the B-1 bombers that were stationed at the base.
In October, after the discovery of a drone with a canister of explosives near another German airbase, the German military raised its Russian sabotage threat assessment to “substantial” — its second-highest level — and warned that the threat was no longer confined to facilities where Ukrainian troops were being trained and to major military installations. More than 30,000 U.S. military personnel are stationed in Germany.

articles.title: US Air Force eyes reviving WWII air bases in the Pacific
articles.snippet: The U.S. Air Force hopes to conduct more than 6,000 aircraft operations annually at airfields on three American islands in the northwest Pacific Ocean.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force hopes to conduct more than 6,000 aircraft operations annually at four airfields on three American islands in the northwest Pacific Ocean, including a major WWII-era airfield that is being refurbished, according to an announcement from the Department of the Air Force.
The department published a notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement that will assess “potential social, economic, and environmental effects” of training and operations at Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport. The islands are part of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, an unincorporated U.S. territory.
The proposed training and exercises will support the Air Force’s Agile Combat Operations concept, which emphasizes dispersal of forces across airfields and the ability to maneuver between them while sustaining operations under a range of conditions, with the goal of thwarting an adversary’s ability to shut down those operations by targeting a single base. ACE, as it’s known, has developed largely in response to the Chinese military’s growing reach and expanding missile arsenal.
The notice said the four airfields provide “a unique opportunity” to support ACE, with infrastructure that varies from “fully developed commercial airfields to expeditionary operating locations.” The three islands are within a few dozen nautical miles of each other, which would allow for training that reflects the complexity of distributed operations while reducing transit time between them. They are less than 100 nautical miles north of the major military bases on Guam, another U.S. territory, which would support the staging and deployment of forces for those exercises.
The three airfields “collectively provide a training environment that enables [the Air Force] to exercise distributed operations, test and employ tailorable force packages, strengthen sustainment and maneuver capabilities, and enhance operational resilience,” the notice reads.
The environmental impact statement will evaluate the potential effects of the proposed activities, which include small, medium and large trainings and exercises held several times a year for a few weeks at a time and consisting of up to 1,200 fixed-wing and 320 rotary-wing operations, like takeoffs and landings, annually at each airfield. It will also assess an alternative scenario with up to 1,400 fixed-wing and 384 rotary-wing operations per airfield annually and a “No Action Alternative.”
The trainings and exercises would be supported by up to 550,000 gallons of fuel at each airfield, up to 1,000 personnel per airfield, the temporary installation of expeditionary infrastructure, the handling of munitions like chaff and flares, as well as support services and pre-and post-training and exercise activities.
The proposed activity comes after several years of work to upgrade the airfields in question, especially the airfields on Tinian, which were built and heavily used during WWII. North Field was inactive after the war and was largely covered with vegetation when the rehabilitation effort began in late 2023. The Air Force also upgraded port and roadway infrastructure, fuel pipelines and airfield surfaces, and utilities to facilitate expanded operations on Tinian.
The airfield rehabilitation efforts have created some questions among Air Force leaders about resourcing and funding, particularly as the war with Iran has placed new demands on the force. Island residents also have misgivings about the projects. While some welcome the investment that the construction and military operations will bring, others have doubts that the increased activity will really benefit the islands’ populations and that the Pentagon will be transparent about its activity and responsive to local concerns.
The Department of the Air Force will hold public meetings this month on Saipan, Tinian and Rota to get feedback on the proposal, with written comments due by Nov. 29. The department plans to produce a draft environmental impact statement for public comment in fall 2027 and a final version in mid-2028.

articles.title: Denmark, Lithuania latest Baltic navies to buy ‘Blocker’ mines through Finnish scheme
articles.snippet: Denmark is the latest country to buy Finland’s “Blocker” naval mines, a day after Lithuania decided to go ahead with its own contract for the weapon.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Denmark is the latest country to buy Finland’s “Blocker” naval mines, a day after Lithuania decided to go ahead with its own contract for the weapon.
The forces of Finland, where the mines are made, and Estonia already operate the proximity sea mines. Estonia bought them in 2021.
The Danish acquisition will take place as part of a pentalateral joint procurement agreement that includes Finland and Lithuania, as well as Germany and Norway, who have not yet publicly announced a contract to buy the device.
Lithuania’s ministry of defense similarly said that its procurement of Blocker was taking place under the Naval Mines Cooperation, a procurement agreement that grew out of a program launched in 2024.
Aside from joint buying, the NMC agreement is meant to “strengthen cooperation on logistics, training, exercises and the lifespan of the systems,” the Danish ministry of defense said.
The Finnish military signed a contract with manufacturer Forcit Defence in June on behalf of the five countries participating in the NMC’s procurement scheme. The contract was worth “hundreds of millions of Euros,” the Finnish government said.
Ten countries signed the pact’s original declaration of intent: Belgium, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Finland and Estonia, all of which are members of NATO.
Germany may still announce a procurement decision this year, German industry publication Hartpunkt reported, citing “well-informed circles.”
“Selecting Finland as the lead nation of the naval mines cooperation project is a reflection of the Finnish Navy’s long-standing capability in naval mining,” the country’s military wrote in a statement.
Forcit Defence advertises the Blocker mine as having the explosive power equivalent to a ton of TNT. It detects ships using a range of sensors.
Naval mines have been front and center in the news this year, with Iran’s use of the technology to block the Strait of Hormuz and hold a large part of global energy supplies hostage in response to the U.S.-Israeli campaign against it.
The Baltic Sea has also become a key point of tension, particularly since 2022, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, the sea is now entirely surrounded by the alliance, except for Russia’s Kaliningrad and Leningrad Oblast coasts. This is a strategic headache for Russia, whose ships must pass through the narrow Danish straits and onward through the Kattegat and Skagerrak to reach the open ocean.
Russia has repeatedly warned that it will not accept being cut off from the Atlantic. “If we do not give them a firm rebuff, the British, French and even the Baltic states will soon become so emboldened that they will try to completely block our country’s access to the seas, at least in the Atlantic basin,” said Nikolai Patrushev, President Vladimir Putin’s aide and chairman of Russia’s Maritime Board, in a February interview with Russian newspaper Argumenty i Fakty and reproduced by the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation. “If this situation cannot be resolved peacefully, the Navy will break through and eliminate the blockade.”

articles.title: How a French frigate’s radical bow design makes for smooth sailing
articles.snippet: The inverted bow on the new FDI frigates makes for better seakeeping, said the former French Navy captain who commanded the lead ship of the class during sea trials.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The inverted bow of France’s Defense and Intervention Frigate makes it one of the most recognizable designs among modern naval ships. The feature also makes for better seakeeping, said the former French Navy captain who commanded the lead ship of the class during sea trials.
The bow shape allows the frigate to plow through waves without impact, and the absence of slamming means much less vibration on board, said Nicolas Guiraud, who commanded the Amiral Ronarc’h frigate for four years until July and is now a marketing director at the vessel’s builder, Naval Group.
“Fewer vibrations mean a ship that ages much more slowly, cracks that won’t form, computer connectors that won’t disconnect,” Guiraud said in an interview at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition in Paris on Nov. 4.
“It also greater comfort for the crew, which isn’t the primary reason, but is still important because people are always part of the equation. And a well-rested sailor is a sailor who will make the right decisions.”
French Navy Chief of Staff Adm. Christophe Cluzel last month told lawmakers that while the FDI faced criticism from competitors, it has proven to be extremely maneuverable and very stable, “contrary to what some comments may have suggested.” Sweden in May announced plans to buy four of the frigates, which are already in use in the French and Hellenic navies.
“This design, which at first raised questions and left many people dubious, is now convincing a lot of people,” Guiraud said. Naval Group presented an 8,000-ton concept drone-carrier frigate at Euronaval that also features an inverted bow, “we believe in it enough to keep proposing it.”
The inverted bow design existed in the 19th century and has made a comeback on support vessels, but is new for a modern frigate, “so there was a real question mark,” according to Guiraud. The French Navy took delivery of its first FDI in October 2025.
Naval Group spent more than a decade analyzing the inverted bow design from the mid-2000s, with extensive tow-tank trials, hydrodynamic modeling, and radar-signature evaluations to address concerns about stability and wetness. The shipbuilder says the inverted bow has a reduced radar profile compared to a flared bow.
The U.S. Navy operates the Zumwalt-class stealth destroyers with an inverted bow, and while that design faced years of stability questions, the commander of the lead ship said in 2020 the vessel handled rough conditions well. The Zumwalt class differs in having a so-called tumblehome design that narrows above the waterline, compared to the French frigate’s flaring hull.
Guiraud’s command of the Amiral Ronarc’h included an extended deployment that ranged from the Arctic Circle to the Equator.
Before the Amiral Ronarc’h, he served on the French multirole FREMM frigate and other ships from previous generations, where he said monitoring hull fatigue was “a central concern.” Feedback so far from the FDI is that structural wear is not an issue, he said.
The FDI’s combination of inverted bow, length-to-width ratio and stabilizing fins means “this platform doesn’t vibrate, it doesn’t experience shocks. And so we believe it will age much better.”
The frigate has a combined diesel and diesel propulsion system that is particularly energy-efficient, and while the FDI is advertised as having a range of 5,000 nautical miles when traveling at 15 knots, Guiraud said it’s actually “a good 10% more.” The maximum speed is 27 knots.
The Amiral Ronarc’h has maintained speeds of 20 knots in sea state 6, which corresponds to very rough seas with waves of 4 to 6 meters (13-20 feet), at times when “we were in a bit of a hurry,” according to Guiraud. The frigate has faced a maximum sea state 7 so far, which corresponds to waves up to 9 meters.
The former frigate commander recounted having to slow “just a little bit” when taking waves head-on in sea state 6, but as soon as the Amiral Ronarc’h adjusted course to take the waves slightly ahead of the beam, it was able to speed up to 20 knots again, “without any particular concern for the integrity of our systems.”
The shape of the bow and stabilizing fins allow the frigate to continue conducting military operations in rough seas. Operating a helicopter or towed array sonar in sea state 5 is “no problem at all,” while doing so in sea state 6 depends on wavelength, swell and wind strength.
The FDI displaces 4,500 metric tons but has the same military capabilities as a 6,000-ton frigate, according to the former commander.
“The main thing is that we continue, despite the decrease in the ship’s size, to maintain the same standards, which is already a very good result. Normally, the smaller the ship, the more complicated it is because the more it moves around.”
“Like any boat, the crew needs to be attentive to sea conditions to adjust their behavior accordingly. But that applies to all boats, and from my perspective, and from the users’ perspective, there’s no difference between a larger vessel and the Amiral Ronarc’h in that regard.”
Guiraud said increased spray caused by the bow shape is not an operational issue, with danger to weapon systems arising from swells in which a mass of water of several tons crashes down on the equipment. The FDI addresses that issue with spray rails on the hull to deflect water.
“There are no waves sweeping across the foredeck. There’s only spray, and our equipment is designed to be waterproof enough to function despite that.”
Guiraud said the bow of the FDI is so high that before the foredeck is submerged, “any boat would have been forced to adjust its course, no matter what. There’s no such thing as a boat that’s immune to having its superstructure submerged by a big wave. It doesn’t exist.”

articles.title: Shield AI to acquire radar maker Echodyne to bust drones
articles.snippet: Shield AI's CEO said the purchase of Echodyne supports the company’s aim to branch into different areas of unmanned systems.
articles.full_text:
Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction announced Thursday — a major financial transaction that expands the prime defense contractors’ drone-warfare capabilities.
Echodyne produces next-generation, solid-state radar systems patented as Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) technology. Its highly advanced systems are flexible and can be easily incorporated into a wide variety of weapons and monitoring systems to detect drones, including high-energy lasers and microwave weapons.
In September, Echodyne was awarded a $250 million contract by the Defense Department’s premier national counter-drone task force, JIATF-401, to provide counter-drone technology to military forces over 36 months.
Speaking to Defense News in July, Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg said demand for counter-drone detecting radar is “red hot” and could grow tenfold by 2030. The company produces technology that can track small quadcopter drones and even over 1,000 objects at a time.
“There is a rush of interest globally for counter-drone,” Frankenberg told Defense News. “The Ukraine war made it obvious to everyone that drones had changed the face of warfare, but the Iran war made it obvious that everything’s at risk.”
The acquisition is a bold new move for Shield AI, which is already well-known as the maker of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, or VTOL drones. The V-Bat became famous for assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in conducting reconnaissance on illicit drug trafficking at sea and enabling law enforcement to make large maritime drug busts.
The company also builds Hivemind autonomy software, which delivers AI pilots to perform multi-agent teaming and swarming across a wide range of unmanned systems, including unmanned aircraft systems, drone boats and spacecraft.
Shield AI CEO Gary Steele said the purchase of Echodyne supports the company’s aim to branch into three different areas of unmanned systems.
“We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” Steele said in a statement.
Frankenberg said in a statement that Shield AI’s mission complements that of Echodyne and that he expects unity of effort to multiply what both companies can deliver.
“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations,” Frankenberg said.
“Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” he continued. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”

articles.title: Popular military air show permanently pulled from RAF Fairford after suspected terror threat
articles.snippet: Over a month after a suspected Iranian plot on RAF Fairford, organizers of the world's largest military air show announced its permanent departure to MOD Boscombe Down.
articles.full_text:
Over a month after a suspected Iranian threat at RAF Fairford rattled officials, one of the world’s biggest annual air shows hosted at the United Kingdom base is permanently relocating to a different installation in the country.
The Royal International Air Tattoo will move from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, to MOD Boscombe Down in Wiltshire after four decades at its longtime home, organizers announced Wednesday.
Following discussions with the Royal Air Force and the U.S. Air Force, organizers canceled the 2026 air show in late May, calling it a difficult decision that was prompted by “uncertainty” over access to RAF Fairford given the base’s involvement with the war in Iran.
The U.S. Air Force housed a dozen B-1B Lancers at RAF Fairford during Operation Epic Fury to use in strikes against Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
But following the suspected terrorist plot targeting the base, the U.S. promptly removed all bombers from the installation and returned them back to their home stations.
British officials said there are “strong indications” that Iran was involved in the late September suspected plot targeting the base, but Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied the accusation on social media. Five men were initially arrested and released on bail. Two men were rearrested and charged under the U.K. National Security Act.
Although the organizers did not cite the plot at RAF Fairford as the reason for the move, they described the relocation essential for the air show’s long-term future.
“The decision to move RIAT to Boscombe Down is about much more than a new location,” RAF Charitable Trust Chief Executive Gavin Gager said in the announcement. “It is about securing the future of the world’s greatest military airshow and the charitable impact it generates for future generations.”
The air show usually attracts more than 150,000 spectators. Its first show at MOD Boscombe Down is scheduled for July 16 to 18.
MOD Boscombe Down is a British military airfield used for aircraft testing and evaluation. It hosts two air squadrons and six units.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia inks first defense ‘cooperation’ agreement with Syria’s new leadership
articles.snippet: “The agreement will likely initially focus on military training, intelligence sharing, equipment transfers and assistance in rebuilding Syria’s armed forces,” one expert told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
BEIRUT — The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has signed its first defense agreement with Syria since the fall of Bashar Assad in Damascus, a step that experts said would likely strengthen the Syrian army’s capabilities.
The agreement “on cooperation between the two countries’ defense ministries” was inked, among other government cooperation agreements, on Wednesday during Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s official press agency said.
Details of the agreement were not disclosed, but experts told Breaking Defense that the move is evidence of growing ties between the two countries. It also highlights a geopolitical reversal in the region, with Al-Sharaa moving closer to Riyadh after years of Syrian allegiance to Saudi rival Iran under Assad.
“The agreement marks another step in Syria’s growing political, economic and military alignment with Saudi Arabia, as Damascus seeks to rebuild its armed forces and strengthen its regional partnerships,” RANE Lead MENA and defense Analyst Freddy Khoueiry told Breaking Defense.
Serhat Süha Çubukçuoğlu, director of the Turkey program at TRENDS Research & Advisory, agreed with Khoueiry, adding that the agreement is “part of Saudi diplomatic, and economic outreach to court Syria and keep it in its sphere of influence.”
The signing comes as Syrian army is trying to rebuild its capabilities after a 14-year civil war that ended in December 2024 with the overthrow of the Assad regime, and as Damascus eyes to end all foreign military presence on its soil.
“The agreement will likely initially focus on military training, intelligence sharing, equipment transfers and assistance in rebuilding Syria’s armed forces,” Khoueiry said.
He added that “over time” the agreement could “pave the way for more direct military cooperation, potentially including Syrian personnel supporting Saudi operations in Yemen” against the Iran-backed Houthi militant group there. Such a step, he cautioned however, “remains speculative and unlikely in the near term.”
And while Syrian foreign minister Asaad al-Shaibani announced last week that Damascus is weighing joining the Saudi-Pakistani-Turkish defense alliance dubbed as Mecca Pact, neither expert viewed the new bilateral announcement necessarily as a step in that direction.
Khoueiry highlighted that the ties between Damscus and Riyadh are already growing, but he didn’t rule out the possibility of Syria joining the Mecca Pact.
“Syria could potentially join by early 2027, although this would depend on negotiations with existing members and Damascus’s willingness to assume the pact’s collective defense obligations, alongside other strategic considerations,” he told Breaking Defense.
Çubukçuoğlu was more hesitant about the possibility, especially since the pact has “a NATO Article 5-type agreement and attack on one is considered attack on all.”
A further complication, he said, was Israeli military operations in Syria, including the occupation of southern Syrian territory. Khoueiry mentioned the perceived Israeli threat as another reason Damascus would strengthen ties with Riyadh, but Çubukçuoğlu said the potential for a fight with Israel could neuter Mecca Pact negotiations.
“I think that’s inconceivable at this point [any] of these countries will enter into a war with Israel to liberate territory,” he concluded.
