articles.title: Key Space Force satellites can’t talk to each other, likely requiring $1B solution: Sources
articles.snippet: To translate between the SpaceX-built SDN Backbone and other Pentagon communications and missile tracking satellites, sources said the Space Force is eyeing 12 or 13 Space Exchange Point birds.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Space Force’s multibillion-dollar effort to build a satellite network that rapidly moves data over high-speed laser links will require an entirely new set of satellites and significant extra funding to connect with other military space systems, Breaking Defense has learned.
In effect, this new group of satellites will serve as translators between different sets of optical waveforms — two or three missile warning/tracking constellations in the short term, and others in the future — in order to ensure multiple systems can talk to each other. That connectivity is a vital part of supporting Trump administration’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative that the network is supposed to help speed into existence, multiple sources said.
The Space Force plans to orbit an “operational prototype” of the Space Data Network Backbone being built by SpaceX by 2027. The large constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) will serve as the data backhaul layer — essentially, the central communications traffic router — of the service’s planned SDN architecture, a space-based network of networks designed to connect sensors to shooters.
The Space Force envisions the SDN as a hybrid constellation comprising military and commercial communications satellites that eventually will be able to share data across missions, including missile warning, tracking and targeting as well as both air- and ground-moving target indication. As a top priority, the SDN will focus on connecting to the Space Development Agency’s (SDA) Tracking Layer satellites for detecting and tracking missiles to be stationed in LEO and Space System Command’s (SSC) similar Resilient Missile Warning and Tracking- Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) birds.
SpaceX won a $2.29 billion contract in May to fast-track development of the SDN Backbone to meet President Donald Trump’s 2028 deadline for implementing Golden Dome. The Space Force has not publicly disclosed how many satellites the backbone will include, but the effort is a restructured version of the earlier MILNET constellation, which a Space Force official said last year would comprise more than 480 satellites.
The SDN Backbone’s central feature is the use of lasers for satellite-to-satellite communications. Laser links, which function via optical communications terminals (OCT) on board satellites, allow the transmission of bigger volumes of data faster and more securely than the radio frequency links carried by traditional communications satellites.
However, SpaceX is using proprietary OCTs on the SDN Backbone satellites, dubbed by the company as “Plasers,” that cannot directly exchange data with those equipping both the SDA and SSC missile warning/tracking satellites, according to multiple industry, former government and current Space Force sources. To complicate matters, these sources said, the OCTs used by SDA and SSC also are incompatible.
To address this lack of connectivity, the Space Force is considering a constellation of 12 to 13 additional satellites that could allow otherwise incompatible OCT payloads to exchange data, two industry sources and one former Space Force official said.
The proposed satellites, known as Space Exchange Points (SEPs) or “translator satellites,” are expected to cost somewhere $12-14 million each, these sources said. That means the satellite project itself would cost north of $100 million, but the sources said that the overall cost of the wider overhaul could reach up to $1 billion — quite the price tag especially at a time the Pentagon is expected to get less funding than it asked for from Congress.
Even aside from the extra costs, however, several sources expressed frustration with the situation with regard to the Space Force’s two new missile warning/tracking constellations, saying it could have been avoided had the Pentagon focused on standardization at an earlier date. Instead, the service is now having to scramble to fix a problem that, the sources emphasized, never needed to happen.
An SSC spokesperson declined to comment on the compatibility of its MEO birds with SDA’s LEO satellites or SpaceX’s Plaser and also declined to comment on the SEP program’s end goals and projected costs. SpaceX did not respond to a detailed inquiry from Breaking Defense.
Different Standards Block Connectivity
The crux of the connectivity problem is that the SpaceX, SDA and SSC OCTs are based on different technical standards governing the precise optical waveforms used, and thus how many gigabits of data per second the laser links can transmit, sources explained.
Part of the reason for the standards mismatch is the decision made some time in 2025 by the Department of the Air Force to flip from using SDA’s Transport Layer of data relay satellites as the SDN backbone to instead relying on SpaceX’s constellation — at the time dubbed MILNET and already in use by the National Reconnaissance Office. By that time, SDA already had been developing both the Transport Layer and the Tracking Layer satellites based on its own open-source OCT standard, a first version of which was published in 2022.
“The optical waveform/terminals on SDA’s Transport Layer and Tracking Layer satellites, which carry the SDA OCT Standard, are not directly compatible with the Plaser waveform,” an SDA official confirmed.
The disconnect between SDA and SSC on OCTs is harder to justify, one former Pentagon official said, given that both developmental programs began at roughly the same time in 2019 — and thus could have worked together to develop compatible OCTs. However, one industry source said, a possible argument for the differences is that SDA has been focused on developing OCTs optimized for its LEO-based satellites, whereas SSC is concentrating on operations in MEO where satellites are farther from the Earth and farther from each other than in LEO.
The Space Force is not unaware of the challenge it faces. G.P. Sandhoo, head of both SDA and the Space Force’s new Missile Warning and Tracking Portfolio Acquisition Executive office, on Oct. 28 told a panel at Silicon Valley Space Week conference in Mountain View, Calif., that his shop will eventually need to figure out how to integrate data from sensors carried by satellites in different orbits, according to an article in Space News.
The SDA official added that “interoperability” between the OCTs for the LEO and MEO missile warning/tracking constellations is currently “being evaluated” by the Space Force.
One solution is simply for the SEP satellites to carry both SDA and SSC standard OCTs, along with software to transmit their data to the SpaceX Plaser and the SDN Backbone satellites.
Another potential solution is for both the LEO and MEO constellations to use a new version of SDA’s optical waveform standard, called v.4.0.0, that potentially could resolve the problem in the future, according to current and former Space Force officials.
That standard was developed in consultation with SSC, the former Space Force official said, and has “two modes:” the first essentially is the same standard SDA is using for “LEO to LEO and LEO to ground” communications; the second would allow LEO to MEO optical data transmission. Thus, it could be used to directly link LEO and MEO missile warning/tracking satellites, and avoid having to add a third OCT payload onto the SEPs.
The SDA official said the version 4 standard “is not yet on contract to be fielded in any SDA Tranches, but is in consideration for Tranche 4.”
Key acronyms in this story
SDN – Space Data Network
LEO – low Earth orbit
MEO – medium Earth orbit
SEP – Space Exchange Point
SDA – Space Development Agency
SSC – Space Systems Command
OCT – Optical Communications Terminal
EST – Enterprise Space Terminal
Translator Sats To The Rescue?
SSC has been working on developing its OCTs, called Enterprise Space Terminals (ESTs), since 2024. At the time, the command described the program as designed “to operationalize a new enterprise waveform designed to communicate in the Beyond Low Earth Orbit (bLEO) regimes,” and estimated it would cost a total of $100 million.
This April, General Atomics and CACI announced they had won Phase 3 awards to develop the EST terminals for “flight hardware” production and demonstration, but provided few other details. And in July, SSC awarded California-based startup K2 Space $22.9 million to host tests of two ESTs on two of its Gravitas satellites.
An SSC spokesperson declined to comment on the technical details of the ESTs, saying only that the “EST payload implements a government owned optical communications standard designed for both long- and short-range communications.”
However, the spokesperson confirmed that prototype ESTs are being designed to equip the future SEP translator satellites
SSC initiated the SEP program on Aug. 13 with awards to five companies worth $12 million each — Amazon LEO for Government, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Rocket Lab and York Space System — to build prototypes. The SEP birds are “specialized spacecraft [that] act as orbital routers, allowing disparate networks and government satellite systems to connect directly” to the SDN backbone, the SSC release said.
To do that, the SSC spokesperson said, the SEP “host vehicles” being built by each of the contractors will be “integrated with” the SDN Backbone — implying that they will be equipped with the SpaceX Plaser — and also will carry the ESTs.
“The five vendors will demonstrate their ability to directly connect their host satellite and associated C2 systems to the existing SDN Backbone architecture; ground-to-ground, ground-to-space, then space-to-space,” the SSC spokesperson added. “Each vendor has their own demonstration schedule and we are planning for demonstrations next calendar year.”
However, the spokesperson declined to comment when specifically asked whether the SEP satellites will be equipped with the Plaser. They also declined to specify whether the government had bought those terminals from SpaceX for the SEP prototypes, or whether each vendor instead was required to do so.
(SpaceX in 2024 said it intended to sell a miniature version of the Plaser to allow third party satellites to connect to Starlink, but it is unclear if any such deals have been made — Muon Space in September 2025 announced a “partnership” to equip its Halo birds with the mini-Plaser but did not specify terms.)
The SSC spokesperson noted that the SEP spacecraft vendors also are working with the EST contractors “to define the interface necessary to host their payloads,” stressing that while the contracts are separate the efforts are complementary.
“Combining these host spacecraft and optical payload elements together, a SEP will allow any external Government system carrying a compatible optical terminal to connect to the SDN Backbone,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson did not, however, provide any information about the SEP constellation’s ultimate size, costs and schedule for deployment.
The concept of a translator satellite is not a new idea. SDA in 2022 was working on the idea to allow data from commercial satellites eventually to flow into the Transport Layer. But questions remain about how difficult it will be to implement.
“Reasonable people will disagree on how difficult it is,” one former Space Force official said. “[T]he technical challenges from the hardware side are pretty straightforward. … But there is some networking translation that has to happen in addition to just the hardware configuration.”
In addition, the official said, the SEP satellites as currently designed are not compatible with either SDA’s Tracking Layer satellites or the Transport Layer, which is being transferred to SSC for further development as a separate so-called enclave of the SDN specifically focused on connecting to legacy military platforms such as fighter jets.
Which raises the question of whether yet more development and funds will be needed.
SDA now is projecting to begin launch of its first operational Tracking Layer satellites, called Tranche 1, next spring, according to a recent article in Space News, representing a two-year delay. Those Tranche 1 birds are to be followed by two more satellite sets — Tranche 2 and 3 — each being designed with improved capabilities. The agency has been projecting Tranche 2 launches to begin in December and initial Tranche 3 launches to start in 2029, but given the delay in Tranche 1 that schedule is now unclear.
As for the Transport Layer, the shift of the program to SSC has thrown the program’s scope, schedule and funding up in the air. The Pentagon’s 2027 budget request shows funding continuing for the Transport Layer’s first two tranches, but no funding for SDA’s earlier planned Tranche 3 and beyond.

articles.title: Europe nears decision on competing hypersonic interceptor programs
articles.snippet: The European Commission is expected to select one of two competing consortia by the end of November to advance development of a European interceptor targeting hypersonic and ballistic missile threats, with a system-level demonstrator targeted for 2030.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Europe is quickly approaching a critical decision point that will help direct its strategy for defending the continent against hypersonic missile threats in the 2030s and beyond.
At the end of the month, the European Commission is expected to downselect either the Hypersonic Interceptor Defence (HYDEF) or Hypersonic Defence Interceptor System (HYDIS) consortiums for the second phase of its Endo-Atmospheric Interceptor (EATMI) program — an effort that aims to develop air defense systems to counter advanced missile threats.
While HYDEF is focused on developing the foundational technologies for a highly maneuverable interceptor, HYDIS has advanced a more defined missile design, known as Aquila.
China and Russia continue to rapidly develop hypersonic missiles, with Chinese systems presenting a growing challenge to European defenses. The weapons can fly at speeds of at least Mach 5 and can maneuver during flight, making their trajectories difficult to predict and giving air defense systems less time to detect, track and intercept them.
To date, both HYDEF and HYDIS consortiums have conducted parallel assessments and design work in support of the first phase of the EATMI program. The Nov. 30 deadline will require the European Commission to move forward with just one provider.
The first phase of EATMI officially wrapped up at the end of October after both consortia’s concepts passed preliminary requirements reviews in the summer. The second phase, expected to begin in 2027, will focus on maturing interceptor technologies and advancing the preliminary design of the complete weapon system.
The European Commission is targeting a system-level demonstrator at technology readiness level 6 by 2030, followed by a development and industrialization phase ahead of an expected in-service date around 2035.
The HYDEF consortium includes the government participation of Spain, Germany, Poland, Belgium and Norway, with an industrial consortium comprising companies from each country. The effort is led by Spanish Missile Systems (SMS), with Diehl Defence acting as technical coordinator. Other participating companies include Nammo, Navantia and GMV.
HYDIS currently includes France, Italy, the Netherlands and also Germany, along with a group of supporting companies comprising MBDA, Saab, Thales and Leonardo, as well as the Netherland’s TNO and Sweden’s FOI government research and development agencies.
The participating companies are organized into teams covering a range of technology areas, including onboard terminal guidance sensors; lethality; communication and datalinks; propulsion systems; aerodynamics and thermal domain; guidance, navigation and control; interceptor maneuverability; and more.
Speaking to the media at the Euronaval expo in Paris on Wednesday, an MBDA official representing HYDIS confirmed that the program’s second phase will focus on moving beyond technology readiness level 3 and toward a “full system demonstrator by the end of the decade.”
Should it be selected, the HYDIS consortium will continue development of the Aquila interceptor, including the capability to launch from surface vessels using the MK41 vertical launch system. Additional focus areas will include affordability and scalable production.
As for HYDEF, the consortium was unable to provide additional details regarding planning for the second phase. However, a Diehl Defence spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the team had completed its first development phase on schedule, with August’s preliminary requirements review and the end-of-October project milestone confirming that all subsystems had exceeded their initial technical maturity targets.
“Building on these results, the HYDEF follow-on consortium is ready to continue development under EATMI and deliver this critical capability for Europe,” the spokesperson added.
As for HYDIS, the consortium confirmed that it plans to continue designing Aquila — a four-stage hypersonic stratospheric interceptor capable of intercepting threats travelling up to Mach 17 at high altitudes.
“We expect the winning solution to be available to European countries [by the end of the decade],” Lionel Mazenq, vice president for incubator programmes at MBDA, said at Euronaval.
Mazenq compared the program’s requirements to the United States’ Glide Phase Interceptor program (GPI) — led by Northrop Grumman and developed in cooperation with Japan — which is designed only to intercept hypersonic glide vehicles.
“The European solution will be the only one to deal with both threats,” Mazenq claimed, adding that the European interceptor will form part of a wider, integrated air and missile defence network.
According to MBDA, the HYDIS solution could provide Europe with “regional shield protection,” covering a 100-kilometer (62-mile) radius with a single launcher. That could mean just one launcher could be deployed to protect the whole of the Netherlands, Mazenq said.
He also illustrated a “continental barrier against hypersonic threats,” suggesting a network of interceptor launchers could be used to protect Europe’s eastern border.
MBDA confirmed that the launchers will need to be networked to a single radar. The company also described ongoing cooperation with the European Space Strategy to use satellite constellations to detect and track missiles from space.
Should it be selected for EATMI Phase 2, the HYDIS follow-on consortium will include an expanded group of European countries. As of September, an additional 13 nations had signed letters of intent or support as part of the consortium’s bid process including Belgium, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Romania and Croatia.
The European Defence Fund (EDF) has pledged €100 million (approximately $112 million USD) for the second phase of the program. Additional funds are expected from the winning consortium. MBDA’s Mazenq confirmed that 11 nations from the HYDIS 2 DP consortium will contribute an additional €133 million (approximately $149 million USD).

articles.title: FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.4 million in crypto from nation-state hackers
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts.
articles.full_text:
FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.4 million in crypto from nation-state hackers
A senior FBI official pleaded guilty to stealing millions in cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by nation-state hackers and theft victims.
Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts.
Yaroch was an FBI Supervisory Special Agent who worked at FBI Headquarters within the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division — with his work focusing on an unnamed nation-state.
He used his seniority to access FBI systems that had the codes and passwords necessary to take cryptocurrency from at least two adversarial nations as well as 10 victims of crimes. In total, he conducted 100 transfers from 79 wallets starting in December 2024. The wallets were connected to 35 different FBI investigations.
Yaroch had hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit card debt, loans and car payments. He paid off several large loans. The Justice Department gained access to his ChatGPT conversations, which showed he planned to buy a vineyard in Portugal and retire.
Yaroch began to make legal arrangements in Portugal and bought plane tickets to the country for him, his wife and his child slated for September. But he ended up confessing to the theft to a DOJ employee in July.
Yaroch told the DOJ employee, who he knew from a previous job, that he was angry about an investigation of a suspect from an unnamed adversarial nation. Yaroch "became frustrated when he could not do more to disrupt this individual's use of cryptocurrency.”
"Yaroch decided to tell [the DOJ employee] about his actions because of the shame and he knew what he did was wrong. Yaroch said it was ‘eating him up inside’ and he wanted to ‘get it off his chest,’” prosecutors said.
Further investigation revealed Yaroch had stolen millions and was often indiscriminate in his theft.
The Justice Department said his thefts ranged from 81 cents to over $580,000 in another fraudulent transfer.
Prosecutors said Yaroch's misuse of the cryptocurrency credentials that he stole from FBI systems “compromised multiple FBI investigations related to both criminal groups and nation state adversaries.”
His actions also exposed the FBI's investigations to the targets who controlled the wallets, compromising their sources and methods.
Yaroch will be sentenced in March.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S. is working on extraditing three suspects from Europe in a case involving more than $100 million in fraud from CEO impersonations.
articles.full_text:
CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say
The Justice Department indicted three men for allegedly scamming companies out of more than $100 million with help from AI.
Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit are accused of pretending to be company CEOs or lawyers and contacting lower-level employees to trick them into sending large payments to bank accounts they controlled.
Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer and Sheetrit was detained in the U.K. in September. The Justice Department said on Thursday that extradition requests for all three men are pending.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the three used artificial intelligence “to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives into sending them and their co-conspirators approximately $129 million.”
Hazan, 54, and Sheetrit, 42, are from Israel while Soall, 41, is Spanish. All three are facing up to 104 years in prison on multiple charges of money laundering, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud and more.
The men allegedly stole nearly $5 million from a hospital in Missouri, $2.6 million from a Rhode Island bank, $2.9 million from a hospital in California, $11.5 million from a tech company in the U.K., $4.6 million from a finance company in Massachusetts and $5.2 million from a Florida pet food company.
According to prosecutors, the conspiracy ran from 2024 to 2026 and involved the three as well as other co-conspirators deploying artificial intelligence as a way to spoof the voices and images of real corporate executives.
Court documents said several incidents involved the three men contacting employees and telling them they needed help with a confidential financial transaction, mimicking the CEO’s voice or image on the call.
To further the scheme, they would tell the employee to speak with lawyers at a large international firm that were working on the transaction — using AI to then make themselves look and sound like those lawyers.
The money was wired to accounts across the U.S., Europe, the UAE and China before the scammers transferred it to cryptocurrency.
Prosecutors said Soall typically impersonated the lawyers and had a script he used to mimic the attorneys. Hazan was in charge of laundering the funds, boasting in one instance of laundering $400 million since 1994, according to court documents. The Justice Department noted that Hazan was previously convicted of bank fraud in 2008.
Senior FBI official James Barnacle said criminals continue to weaponize emerging technology like artificial intelligence.
“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large scale fraud,” he said.
The FBI urged other companies that may have been victims to come forward.
Jonathan Greig

articles.title: EU accuses TikTok of trapping users in harmful ‘rabbit holes’
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The European Commission accused TikTok on Friday of failing to prevent its recommendation algorithm from drawing users into “rabbit holes” of content about sadness, self-harm and body image.
articles.full_text:
EU accuses TikTok of trapping users in harmful ‘rabbit holes’
The European Commission accused TikTok on Friday of failing to prevent its recommendation algorithm from drawing users into “rabbit holes” of content about sadness, self-harm and body image.
The preliminary findings that TikTok violated the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) come amid focus on both sides of the Atlantic on whether and how social media platforms are endangering young users.
European officials said their findings were the first time EU regulators have directly challenged the engagement-based recommendation system of a major social media platform, and, to their knowledge, was the first enforcement action of its kind worldwide.
The investigation was directly “addressing a business model” built primarily on user engagement, a Commission official told journalists.
TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed “shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image,” stated the European Commission.
“The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image.”
Brussels said TikTok had identified some of the issues it was flagging in its own risk assessments, but that its investigators found the company had failed to properly analyze those risks and set appropriate safeguards.
The findings are not final and TikTok has a chance to review the Commission’s evidence and challenge its findings.
If the DSA violations are confirmed the company could face a fine of up to 6% of its annual global revenue. The company does not publish its global revenue, nor does its parent company ByteDance.
Rabbit holes
European officials stressed the case was not about removing content, and said investigators deliberately focused on videos that were neither illegal nor against TikTok’s own rules, which one official described as the “least harmful” category of content.
Citing trends including “what I eat in a day” and “SkinnyTok,” officials said the legal content could appear harmless in isolation but became damaging through repetition, particularly for young and vulnerable users.
It follows U.S. senators in August demanding answers from TikTok over the death of Chase Nasca, a 16-year-old who took his own life in February 2022 after viewing a stream of content related to sadness and suicide.
An internal TikTok review, reported last year by Bloomberg, revealed Nasca was part of a control group comprising about 10% of the platform’s user base in which it withheld design changes intended to prevent repeated exposure to harmful subjects.
“If you get a chain of hundreds or even thousands of videos of the same kind of content, this drives people in what we call a rabbit hole, and this has a negative impact on people's mental well-being,” a European Commission official said on Friday.
TikTok’s own tools to break the loops do not work, according to the Commission, which said the platform’s “dispersion” techniques to diversify the feed are ineffective, refreshing the feed only helps briefly, and tapping “not interested” stops working after a while.
In particular, the Commission said it wants TikTok to base its algorithmic recommendations on what users explicitly say they want rather than on implicit signals such as how long they view videos for.
They said they spent two and a half years developing “amongst the world’s most advanced investigatory infrastructures,” but that specific testing methods were necessarily secret to prevent platforms from gaming the tools.
They said they obtained the company’s internal documents and data, and analyzed around 20,000 videos with help from psychologists, psychiatrists and experts in system design. The testing “didn't really need access to the exact algorithm. We had enough information without it,” one official said.
A spokesperson for TikTok, which has the right to check and challenge the Commission’s evidence, said: “The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.
“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience,” they added.
Friday’s findings are the third the Commission has issued against TikTok this year, following one in February challenging addictive design features and another in July regarding protections on minors’ accounts.
Officials distinguished this case as being focused on the platform’s recommendation system rather than issues related to notifications or endless scrolling. They said it went further than TikTok’s recent settlement in Alabama, which “does not go as deep” into the recommendation system.
They acknowledged other platforms similarly push users into rabbit holes and said the Commission was “looking more widely beyond TikTok,” although they declined to comment beyond TikTok.
The Commission described the case as a “scene setter” for its proposed KIDS Act, introduced in September, which would prohibit platforms from relying solely on engagement signals to recommend content to children — a provision officials said was directly inspired by its TikTok investigation.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.snippet: The library system, which has 66 branches serving the borough’s 2.3 million residents, published multiple alerts on Wednesday confirming that the disruption was caused by a ransomware attack.
articles.full_text:
Queens Public Library says ransomware attack disrupted Wi-Fi, on-site computers
The Queens Public Library in New York City said a ransomware gang has encrypted its systems and shut down many of its digital services.
The library system, which has 66 branches serving the borough’s 2.3 million residents, published multiple alerts on Wednesday confirming that the disruption was caused by a ransomware attack.
In a statement on social media, the library said on-site computers, check-out and return machines, WiFi access, digital media services and its mobile app are all down due to the attack.
“All QPL locations remain open as scheduled; however, certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted,” they said. “We are working closely with law enforcement and cybersecurity experts to address this situation, and we will keep you informed.”
The library system initially warned of outages on Wednesday afternoon before confirming the ransomware attack hours later.
New York City officials did not respond to requests for comment. Queens Public Library is one of the largest library systems in the country, offering free access to more than 5 million books in 50 languages.
It operates dozens of learning centers in public housing complexes across the borough as well as several mobile libraries.
No ransomware gang has taken credit for the attack as of Thursday evening. Ransomware gangs previously caused significant damage to dozens of public libraries around the world, including Seattle Public Library as well as several city and county library systems.
The cybercriminal gangs use the demand for e-books and critical services as a wedge to make organizations pay.
In 2023, ransomware gangs destroyed the systems of The British Library, the national library of the United Kingdom. The Toronto Public Library spent months recovering from a ransomware attack in 2023 that they called a “crime scene.”
Library systems also carry significant amounts of data on local populations. A ransomware attack on Washington State’s Pierce County Library System last year exposed the information of more than 340,000 people.

articles.title: Social media giants sue California to overturn law shielding kids 15 and under from compulsive use
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Google, Meta and TikTok each filed suit in federal court against an incoming California law that blocks platforms from deploying features considered “psychologically exploitative.”
articles.full_text:
Social media giants sue California to overturn law shielding kids 15 and under from compulsive use
Meta, TikTok and Google are suing California to prevent enforcement of a new law that creates safeguards to protect children 15 and younger from becoming addicted to the platforms.
Assembly Bill 1709 is set to take effect on January 1 and blocks platforms from deploying features the law calls “psychologically exploitative.”
The trio of tech giants — whose brands include Instagram, Facebook and YouTube — have said the law improperly allows the state to make decisions that should be left to parents.
The firms on Wednesday filed three coordinated but separate lawsuits in California federal courts. Google parent Alphabet filed in San Jose, Meta in San Francisco and TikTok in Los Angeles.
The companies argue the law is unconstitutional because it violates freedom of speech principles.
The tech firms also assert that the soon to be implemented law ignores legal protections blocking platforms from being held liable for user content. That law, known as Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, has long been controversial, with many arguing that it amplifies algorithms and keeps big tech from being held accountable for harms.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a widely reported statement that he is “committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online.”
The law was signed in September by Governor Gavin Newsom, who reportedly said at the time that the state would not “stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk."
A spokesperson for Google said in a statement that the firm believes “parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control.”
“Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
